headline: SUNDAY EDITION. Forty-eight hours after Chair Warsh made a September HIKE the base case at 59%, nothing has challenged it: no clarification, no Fed speaker, no Sunday-show principal. The Venezuela oil deal DID develop - and toward incoherence, with Caracas saying 25 years against Washington's 100 and four incompatible structures circulating. The overlooked Friday print: Chicago's factory barometer collapsed 10.5 points to 47.1
client_frame_short:
The question you will get Monday is whether Friday's Fed news got worse over the weekend. It did not. Two days after the new Chair told Jackson Hole that inflation is the Fed's problem to own - which moved the odds of a September rate HIKE to 59% from 38% in a single afternoon - there has been no clarification, no Fed official speaking, and no walk-back. **The market's view that the Fed's next move is up rather than down is now two days old and unchallenged.**

Nothing here needs a decision from you. One thing is worth flagging because it cuts the other way and almost nobody noticed it. Friday morning the Chicago factory survey collapsed more than 10 points to 47.1, well into contraction. Tuesday's national manufacturing number is still expected at about 55. If the national reading follows Chicago down, the case for raising rates gets harder in a hurry.
client_frame:
The most useful thing I can tell you about this weekend is what did not happen. Friday's Jackson Hole speech was the largest hawkish repricing of the year, and in the 48 hours since, no Fed official has spoken, no clarification or walk-back has appeared, and no Fed, Treasury, State or Energy principal is booked on the Sunday shows - Face the Nation's confirmed lineup is two legislators and an election-law expert. That silence is itself informative. When a central bank makes a large move in expectations and then declines to soften it over a weekend, the move is usually intended. Adam Posen of the Peterson Institute put the consequence bluntly: you are basically setting yourself up so that if you don't hike in September, people may ask what's going on. The sell side is genuinely split - Morgan Stanley's Michael Gapen calls it a close call but still expects a hold because he thinks inflation is decelerating, and Greg Gizzi expects a hold too.

So the rate market's position is unchanged from what I sent you yesterday, and I will name a disclosure rather than hide it: the CME probability API was down this morning, failing three times at authentication, so today's figures were re-parsed from the raw payload we saved Friday. That is the correct cohort for a Sunday anyway, since nothing has settled since Friday's close, but you should know the provenance. A 25bp hike on September 16 sits at 59.00%, October cumulative at 71.71%, December at 89.46%, and December's odds of two or more hikes at 51.81% against 29.84% on Thursday. Cut probability is exactly zero at every meeting through January 2027. Independent weekend prints on the September number span 55.7% to about 60%, so ours is inside the range rather than an outlier.

Now the number I owe you, because we missed it yesterday and it is the best piece of counter-evidence available. The Chicago Business Barometer printed Friday morning at 47.1, down 10.5 points from 57.6 - a collapse from expansion into contraction in one month, confirmed on both the ISM-Chicago and MNI releases. Tuesday's national ISM manufacturing consensus is 55.1 against a 55.6 prior, which means the national forecast has not moved at all for it. I want to be careful here rather than dramatic: Chicago is the noisiest regional survey in the set and it has produced false signals before, so this is an asymmetry, not a forecast. But it is the first hard datapoint pointing away from the hike, it arrives ten days before the FOMC, and Friday's August employment report - consensus plus 50,000 on a Dow Jones survey of eleven economists, with estimates ranging from plus 15,000 to plus 90,000 - is the number that resolves it.

The one story that genuinely moved this weekend is the Venezuela oil agreement, and it moved in the direction of less clarity rather than more. Interim President Delcy Rodriguez said in a Saturday night television address that the deal runs 25 years across 17 fields with an initial target above 1.5 million barrels a day; a State Department official told TIME it grants 100-year rights and gives the US 55% of output split between equity and at-cost offtake; officials briefing CNN described 55% equity with Venezuela at 45%. Those are four mutually incompatible structures, and as of this morning there is still no primary document - nothing on the White House presidential-actions page, nothing in State Department press releases. The 25-year term is what Venezuelan hydrocarbons law permits; the 100-year construct has no obvious lawful route. Chevron is reportedly close to migrating all its Venezuelan joint ventures with a signing expected Wednesday. Analysts are unanimous on timing: Rystad's Claudio Galimberti says benefits arrive mostly in the medium to long term, GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan says changes to fuel prices won't happen overnight or even in months, and IESA's Oswaldo Felizzola says at least three or four years. Meanwhile the pump price is $4.08 a gallon as of Saturday against $3.20 a year ago. For clients: the frame this weekend is that the Fed has stopped pretending its next move might be a cut and has spent two days not taking it back - so Friday's jobs report and Tuesday's manufacturing number now matter more than any headline, and a deal that gets announced four different ways with no document attached is a reminder that the gap between an announcement and a barrel of oil is measured in years.

geo_headlines: THE MOST IMPORTANT NUMBER IN TODAY'S BRIEF IS ONE WE MISSED YESTERDAY, AND IT ARGUES AGAINST THE HIKE. The MNI Chicago Business Barometer printed FRIDAY at 9:45 ET: 47.1, DOWN 10.5 points from 57.6 in July - a fall from solid expansion into contraction in a single month. It is dual-sourced to the ISM-Chicago release and MNI's own write-up, and the issuer publication calendar confirms Aug 28 as the release date, with the next print Sept 30. Two things follow. First, run #166 did not carry this, and some aggregators still show a spurious Aug 31 row with a 57.8 figure, which is wrong. Second and far more important: Tuesday's national ISM manufacturing consensus is 55.1 against a 55.6 prior, so the national forecast has not repriced one point for it. We are deliberately not overstating this - Chicago is the noisiest regional survey in the set and has produced false signals before, so this is an ASYMMETRY rather than a forecast. But it is the first hard datapoint pointing away from a September hike, and it lands ten days before the FOMC.

WHAT DID NOT HAPPEN THIS WEEKEND IS THE STORY ON THE FED. Across a window from Saturday 7am ET to Sunday 7am ET: no Warsh clarification, correction or follow-up; no other Fed official on the record; and no Fed, Treasury, State or Energy principal located on any Sunday show - Face the Nation's confirmed Aug 30 lineup is Senator Blumenthal, Representative James and an election-law expert. When a central bank produces the largest hawkish repricing of the year and then spends 48 hours declining to soften it, the move reads as intended. Adam Posen of the Peterson Institute framed the trap: you are basically setting yourself up so that if you don't hike in September, people may ask what's going on. The sell side is split rather than converted - Morgan Stanley's Michael Gapen calls September a close call but expects a hold because he sees inflation decelerating, Greg Gizzi expects a hold, and Aptus's John Luke Tyner takes the other side, saying underlying inflation trends have not meaningfully improved. Kenneth Rogoff pushed back on Warsh's AI-driven non-inflationary-growth theme: the idea that AI magically solves everything is a bit overblown.

WE ARE DISCLOSING A DATA OUTAGE RATHER THAN QUIETLY SHIPPING AROUND IT. The CME FedWatch API is DOWN this morning. Our re-fetch failed three consecutive times at the OAuth token endpoint with HTTP 400 and a server_error body - a fault on CME's side, not a credential problem. What we ship is the 2026-08-28 cohort re-parsed this run from the raw CME response payload we saved Friday, with every probability array re-verified from scratch: all four meetings sum to 1.0000 and all four carry reportingDt 2026-08-28. Because a Sunday build requires Friday's cohort anyway - no session has settled since - nothing here is stale, but the provenance is a saved payload rather than a live call and you are entitled to know that. The substance is unchanged: a September 16 HIKE at 59.00% against 41.00% hold, October cumulative 71.71%, December 89.46%, January 2027 92.12%, and December's odds of TWO OR MORE hikes at 51.81% from 29.84% Thursday. Cut probability is exactly ZERO at every meeting through January 2027. Independent weekend prints on September span 55.7% at CNBC to about 60% at AFR, TheStreet and Morningstar, so 59.00% is inside the range.

THE VENEZUELA DEAL DEVELOPED OVER THE WEEKEND, AND IT DEVELOPED TOWARD INCOHERENCE. Four mutually incompatible descriptions of the same agreement are now in circulation. Interim President Delcy Rodriguez, in a Saturday night address on state television, said the deal runs 25 YEARS across 17 strategic fields with an initial target above 1.5 million barrels a day plus eight greenfield blocks, projecting about $209 billion of state revenue at $65 a barrel and roughly $19 a barrel to Venezuela, and insisted Caracas keeps ownership and sovereignty. A State Department official told TIME the deal grants 100-YEAR rights and gives the US 55% of the new company's OUTPUT, split between equity and guaranteed at-cost offtake. Officials briefing CNN described 55% EQUITY with a 45% Venezuelan interest. Those are different economics, not different phrasings. The 25-year term is precisely what Venezuela's hydrocarbons law permits for mixed companies; the 100-year construct has no obvious lawful route. And the critical negative finding, checked this morning: there is STILL no primary document - nothing on the White House presidential-actions page for Aug 29 or 30, nothing in State Department press releases, no published Venezuelan decree. The only on-the-record US statement remains Secretary Rubio's Friday evening post. No OPEC reaction, no denial, no walk-back.

THE OIL MECHANICS THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE HEADLINE: Chevron is reportedly close to finalising the migration of ALL its Venezuelan joint ventures into the country's new energy framework, including an asset swap letting Petropiar, its largest Venezuelan project, expand into the neighbouring Ayacucho 8 block, with the signing expected to be announced WEDNESDAY - two sources to Reuters, read through a mirror, so reported rather than primary-confirmed, and Chevron declined to comment. Rodriguez says Venezuela signs with several companies next week. On timing, the analysts are unanimous and it is the single most client-useful part of this story: Rystad's chief economist Claudio Galimberti says benefits arrive mostly in the medium to long term and consumers should factor in several quarters and in many cases years; GasBuddy's Patrick De Haan says drilling and pumping that oil will take a very long time and changes to fuel prices won't happen overnight or even in months, and warns a 100-year contract could face legal challenge or be hard to enforce; IESA's Oswaldo Felizzola says the increase in production won't be seen for at least three or four years. Venezuela currently produces about 1.25 million barrels a day. The US national average pump price was $4.08 a gallon as of Saturday against $3.20 a year earlier. No sell-side barrel-or-dollar estimate of the deal's price impact was published in the window, and we are not manufacturing one.

THE CURVE AND THE COMMODITY COMPLEX, RE-DERIVED THIS MORNING RATHER THAN CARRIED. The 2-year settled 4.352%, +11.4bp, against a 10-year at 4.717%, +4.3bp, so 2s10s is 36.5bp from 43.6bp - 7.1bp of bear flattening, which is the shape that says policy rather than inflation expectations. The 5-year settled 4.49% and the 30-year 5.21%, up just 1.1bp. Yesterday we logged TradingEconomics' dedicated 10Y page DEGRADED for reading 4.69 when its own overview table and four wires read 4.72; this run all three TE surfaces AGREE at 4.7170, so that defect has CLEARED and was a lagged intraday snapshot rather than a persistent fault. A NEW defect replaces it: TE's Brent page contradicted ITSELF, with a data table at 88.290 and narrative text on the same page saying Brent fell to $89.3. The narrative is right - the 88.29 print is a contract-roll artefact, since Brent October expires Aug 31 - and we ship the 89.31 October settle, corroborated independently. WTI settled 83.40, -$0.13, on Barchart's contract page and energynow, which also gives the citable weekly basis we lacked yesterday: down $3.66 or 4.2% from the prior Friday's $87.06 close.

GEOPOLITICS WAS LOW-DELTA AND WE ARE REPORTING THAT PLAINLY RATHER THAN PADDING IT. Hormuz is a status quo of severe degradation rather than a new disruption: UKMTO kept its threat assessment at SEVERE for vessels transiting the strait, with SUBSTANTIAL across the Gulf of Oman, Gulf of Aden and Bab el Mandeb, and said traffic remains significantly reduced despite a brief late-June recovery. One Saturday desk snapshot circulating with vessel counts and a Brent print is sourced to an outlet on our excluded list and is therefore dropped rather than repeated. A White House meeting is flagged for the afternoon of Tuesday Sept 1. In Ukraine, the death toll from the Russian strike on a munitions depot near Kyiv rose through Saturday from 37 to 38 - the strike itself began before our window - with the overnight package one Oniks, one Iskander-M and 267 drones across 15 locations, and 233 drones downed or jammed. No energy-export or port infrastructure was reported damaged, so there is no obvious crude or grain transmission. Nothing new on Canada's Sept 8 counter-tariffs, nothing new on semiconductor tariffs, nothing new on the Sept 30 funding deadline.

THE WEEKEND TAPE ITSELF, AND WHAT THE ONE MARKET THAT WAS OPEN SAID: bitcoin. Saturday's UTC bar closed 78233.93, +0.51%, on a high of 78351 and a low of 77345.28 - a full 24-hour range of about 1.3%, which is unusually tight for this asset and says the weekend produced no forced flows in the only continuously traded thing on our board. Live spot was 78140.865 at 11:13 UTC this morning, down 0.12% from that close. Net of everything, bitcoin is roughly 0.4% above where it sat before Friday's speech and +24.5% on the month. Elsewhere the corporate tape was genuinely empty and we checked specifically: no M&A announcement inside the window, no in-window bankruptcy filing, no earnings pre-announcements or guidance cuts, and no follow-up whatsoever on the PayPal-Stripe collapse. Asia produced no weekend catalyst either - no Japanese or Korean release, no BOJ or BOK communication - which leaves Monday's China NBS PMI as the first real event. July was 49.2, the first contraction since February, and a Friday Reuters poll expects a second consecutive contraction. Between that and Chicago at 47.1, global manufacturing is the thread to pull this week.
